title: "Writing Your Own Modules"
unit: 2
cluster: "Writing Modules"
---

A function written in one Python file is often useful in other programs. Any
Python file can be imported as a module.

In this lesson, we'll learn how to:

* import a Python file as a module
* see what happens when a module is imported more than once
* reimport a module after changing it

## Importing a Python file

Let's create a python file `mymodule.py` with the following content.

```python
%%file mymodule.py

print("BEGIN mymodule")
x = 2

def add(a, b):
    return a + b

print(add(3, 4))
print("END mymodule")
```

```text
Writing mymodule.py
```

Let's see what happens when we run this file as a script:

```python
!python mymodule.py
```

```text
BEGIN mymodule
7
END mymodule
```

Let's see what happens when we import this file as a module.

```python
import mymodule
```

```text
BEGIN mymodule
7
END mymodule
```

```python
mymodule.x
```

```text
2
```

```python
mymodule.add(10, 20)
```

```text
30
```

As you can see, a python file can be imported as a module and the code in that
file gets executed, just the same way as when it is run as a script.

The output would be the same if we import the module from another python file
or the program is passed directly from python command-line[^python-c].

```python
!python -c "import mymodule; print(mymodule.add(10, 20))"
```

```text
BEGIN mymodule
7
END mymodule
30
```

[^python-c]: The python command-line flag `-c` allows passing the program
directly from the command line. It is handy to quickly try some small snippets
of code. When the code is multiple statements, they are usually separated by a
semicolon.

## Reimporting a module

The code of the module is executed only once even if the module is imported
more than once.

```python
import mymodule
import mymodule
```

That means, if you make some changes to the file of a module after it is
imported, you'll not see the changes even if you import it again.

::: {.callout-warning}
This is especially annoying when you are working in a Jupyter notebook.
:::

The work-around to that issue is to reimport a module using `importlib`.

```python
import mymodule

# and make some changes to mymodule.py

import importlib
importlib.reload(mymodule)
```

```text
BEGIN mymodule
7
END mymodule
<module 'mymodule' from '/home/anand/python/mymodule.py'>
```

Use a `%%file` cell to create `words.py` with a function `count_words()` that
takes a sentence and returns the number of words in it. Import the `words`
module and use the function. It should produce these results:

```python
import words
words.count_words("Python programs can read text files.")
```

```text
6
```

```python
words.count_words("Anything that can go wrong, will go wrong.")
```

```text
8
```

## Summary

A Python file can be imported as a module; the code in the file runs the
first time it is imported, just as when the file is run as a script.

| Form or rule | Meaning |
|--------------|---------|
| `import mymodule` | runs `mymodule.py` and makes the module available |
| `mymodule.add(10, 20)` | calls a function defined in `mymodule.py` |
| `mymodule.x` | the value of a variable defined in `mymodule.py` |
| a second `import mymodule` | does not run the file again |
| `importlib.reload(mymodule)` | runs the file again and loads the changes |
| `python -c "import mymodule"` | runs a program given on the command line |
